title: Why I built my portfolio to look like a terminal
body:
In one of my recent class projects, we built a CLI, a program you use entirely from the terminal. I expected it to feel old school, but I ended up really enjoying it. There's something satisfying about typing a command and getting exactly what you asked for.

So when it was time to build my portfolio, I didn't want to start from scratch with a design that had nothing to do with what I'd been learning. I like carrying forward what I learn into the next thing I build, and the terminal felt like the perfect fit. Why not make my portfolio look and feel like one?

That's how this site came together. The navigation is written like shell commands (cd /about-me, ls /projects), every page opens with a command like you're running it yourself, and the home page has a mini terminal where you can type commands like help or projects to move around. I built it with Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, working alongside an AI coding agent.

The biggest thing I learned is that a theme isn't just about looks. Making something feel like a terminal meant thinking about how people actually move around a site, and making sure it still works on a phone, where typing commands isn't always easy.

I'm going to keep building on this, so try typing help on the home page and see what's there.

title: What working with an AI coding agent taught me
body:
I recently built my portfolio with an AI coding agent. I'd describe what I wanted in plain English, and it would plan the work, write the code, and test it. I expected the hard part to be getting good code out of it. The hard part turned out to be knowing when to question it.

It was genuinely impressive in places. Before writing a single line, it checked the documentation for the exact framework version I was using and caught a breaking change I didn't know existed. It ran checks after every step, so problems surfaced early instead of piling up at the end.

But it also took shortcuts, and spotting them was where I learned the most. It hardcoded a value that would have quietly broken my design if I ever changed one line of text. It copied the same validation logic into two different files instead of sharing it. When it helped write my project descriptions, it polished them just a little too much, so I went back and made sure every line was something I could stand behind.

My takeaway: an AI agent is fast, but it only knows what you tell it, and it won't always notice its own shortcuts. The habits that helped me most were simple. Ask it to plan before it codes. Ask it to list problems before it fixes them. Read what it writes.

It didn't replace my thinking. It moved it: less time typing, more time reviewing, deciding, and asking why.
